documents.body:
m6 is an integrated system for building and serving websites. It covers the whole stack — from authoring content in Markdown to writing bytes to a network socket — under one roof, with a single config format and a unified set of concepts.

Under the hood it's a family of small Unix processes, each with one job, communicating over Unix sockets. What makes it more than a collection of parts is that the pieces are designed to work together: the renderer produces output the cache can serve directly, and one request, POST /genid, makes every backend read new content and empties the cache. The result is a system that's simpler to reason about than a stack assembled from separate tools, and fast because none of the layers work against each other.

There's no framework to install, no build pipeline to configure, and no daemon to babysit — systemd handles process management in production, and a shell script handles it in development.

This guide gets you from zero to a running local site.

Prerequisites

You'll need Rust (stable) and mkcert for local TLS:

cargo install m6-http m6-html m6-file
mkcert -install && mkcert localhost 127.0.0.1

The mkcert command writes localhost+1.pem and localhost+1-key.pem in the current directory. The examples do not read those two files. Each example's dev.sh runs examples/dev-keys.sh, which writes dev.pem and dev-key.pem to dev/ in a private per-user directory (@M6_DEV_HOME@ in the configs), and the system config refers to those.

Clone the examples

git clone https://github.com/m6/m6-examples
cd m6-examples/examples/01-static

Start the site

./dev.sh

Open https://localhost:8443 in your browser. That's it.

What just happened?

flowchart LR
    Browser --"HTTPS :8443"--> mhttp["m6-http"]
    subgraph "m6 stack"
        mhtml["m6-html"]
        mfile["m6-file"]
    end
    mhttp --"Unix socket"--> mhtml
    mhttp --"Unix socket"--> mfile

The dev script started three processes:

  • m6-html — renders HTML from Tera templates and JSON data files. Listening on a Unix socket.
  • m6-file — serves static assets from the filesystem. Listening on a Unix socket.
  • m6-http — the only public-facing process. Its primary job is its in-memory response cache. On a cache hit, it writes pre-rendered, pre-compressed bytes directly to the network socket — m6-html and m6-file are not contacted at all. On a cache miss, it routes the request to the right backend, stores the response, and serves all future requests for that URL from RAM.

All three read from the same site directory. m6-http routes based on site.toml. m6-html routes based on configs/m6-html.conf. After the first request to any page, subsequent requests never touch m6-html or m6-file.

The site directory

01-static/
├── site.toml           ← routing and backend declarations
├── configs/
│   ├── m6-html.conf    ← which templates render which paths
│   └── m6-file.conf    ← which URL prefixes map to which filesystem roots
├── templates/
│   ├── base.html
│   ├── home.html
│   └── page.html
├── assets/
│   └── style.css
└── data/
    └── site.json       ← global template variables (site name, nav, etc.)

No binary blobs. No generated files. Everything you see is what you deploy.

Editing content

Open data/site.json and change site_name. Then stop the stack with Ctrl-C and run ./dev.sh again. m6 reads its files once, at start, so a change shows after a restart, which also empties m6-http's cache. Reload your browser tab.

Add a page

Add a route to configs/m6-html.conf:

[[route]]
path     = "/contact"
template = "templates/page.html"
params   = ["data/contact.json"]

Create data/contact.json:

{ "title": "Contact", "body": "<p>hello@example.com</p>" }

Restart the stack, and https://localhost:8443/contact is live.

Next steps

  • Guide 00 — Prerequisites — install binaries, set up local TLS
  • Guide 01 — Static Site — templates, assets, hand-authored JSON
  • Guide 02 — Blog with m6-md — Markdown source files rendered to JSON
  • Guide 03 — Contact Form — custom renderer, SMTP
  • Guide 04 — Login and Protected Pages — JWT auth, HttpOnly cookies
  • Guide 05 — CMS Blog — full CMS with draft/publish workflow
  • Guide 06 — Production with systemd — unit files, scaling, crash recovery
  • Guide 07 — Dev to Production — same config, two environments

The architecture overview explains how the pieces fit together.

Next: m6 Architecture →

documents.body:
You could build what m6 does from parts: a Markdown converter, a template engine, a reverse proxy, a caching layer, an auth service. nginx, Varnish, PHP, Pandoc — the parts exist. People have been assembling them for decades. Each piece is well-understood in isolation.

The problem is the seams. Every integration point is a configuration file in a different format, a different concept of what a "route" is, a different way to invalidate a cache, a different log format, a different security model. The tools don't share a mental model, so you carry several of them simultaneously. Debugging means knowing which layer ate the request. Optimising means understanding five different caching models.

m6 is a different approach. It's an integrated system that thinks about the whole stack — from authoring pages in Markdown to writing bytes to a network socket — and handles all of it under one roof, with a single set of concepts, a single config format, and a unified model of how content moves from source to browser.

The integration is what makes the developer experience simpler. It's also what makes the system fast: because the cache layer knows exactly which content files each URL depends on, it can drop every stale page in one step when content changes, with one number to track and nothing to match. Because the rendering layer speaks directly to the cache layer's expectations, responses arrive already compressed and ready to serve. No adapter overhead, no translation, no impedance mismatch.

This is still a collection of small Unix processes. Each has one job. They communicate over Unix sockets. You wire them together with a config file. But the point isn't the processes — the point is that the whole journey, from the Markdown file on disk to the bytes on the wire, is a single coherent system.

The processes

flowchart LR
    Browser --"HTTPS"--> mhttp["m6-http\n(cache + router)"]
    subgraph "Backends (Unix sockets)"
        mhtml["m6-html"]
        mfile["m6-file"]
        mauth["m6-auth"]
        custom["Custom Renderer"]
    end
    mhttp --"cache miss only"--> mhtml
    mhttp --"cache miss only"--> mfile
    mhttp --"credential ops"--> mauth
    mhttp --"cache miss only"--> custom

m6-http is the only process that listens on a public port. Its primary job — the one that determines real-world performance — is its in-memory response cache. Most requests in production never reach a backend at all. m6-http serves them directly from RAM: a complete HTTP response, fully rendered, already compressed to brotli or gzip, with all headers pre-formed. On a cache hit, m6-http does nothing except write bytes to the network socket.

On a cache miss, m6-http routes the request to the appropriate backend pool, gets a rendered response back, stores it in the cache if the response is cacheable, and returns it to the client. Subsequent requests for the same resource hit the cache.

m6-http also terminates TLS, enforces route-level authentication, and fetches styled error pages from m6-html when backends fail. It does not start, stop, or monitor other processes — that's systemd's job.

m6-html renders HTML from Tera templates and JSON data files. Each instance listens on a Unix socket. Its entire application logic is: match path → load params files → merge global params → render template → compress → respond. No database, no sessions, no side effects.

m6-file serves files from the filesystem. Similar socket convention to m6-html, but no templates, no params. Just path resolution with traversal protection and content-type detection.

m6-auth issues and verifies JWTs, manages credentials and ACLs. It listens on two sockets: the login socket for login, token refresh and logout, and a check socket that answers POST /check. m6-http asks the check socket who a caller is whenever a route has a require, so a role or group change takes effect without a new token. The check is one local socket round trip and only protected routes pay it.

User-supplied renderers are ordinary HTTP/1.1+ servers. Declared as backends in site.toml. Managed by systemd. A Rust renderer links m6-core, which supplies the parts of a service (routing, the request dictionary, templates, the event-loop pieces) and leaves the loop and the handlers to the renderer, but any language works.

Tiers

flowchart TD
    subgraph "Tier 1 — Static"
        T1H["m6-http"] --- T1Html["m6-html"]
        T1H --- T1File["m6-file"]
    end
    subgraph "Tier 2 — Generated Static"
        T2H["m6-http"] --- T2Html["m6-html"]
        T2H --- T2File["m6-file"]
        T2Md["m6-md (external)"] --> T2Data[("data JSON")]
        T2Data --> T2Html
    end
    subgraph "Tier 3 — Dynamic"
        T3H["m6-http"] --- T3Html["m6-html"]
        T3H --- T3File["m6-file"]
        T3H --- T3R["custom renderer"]
    end

m6 sites fall into three tiers based on what you actually need:

Tier 1 — Static. m6-http + m6-html + m6-file. Templates, configs, assets, and hand-authored JSON. No build step. Deployed by copying files. This covers a lot of ground: marketing sites, documentation, portfolios.

Tier 2 — Generated static. Same as tier 1, but content JSON is produced by an external tool. m6-md converts Markdown files with TOML frontmatter into the { "documents": [...] } format m6-html expects. Other tools can produce the same format. m6 itself has no opinion about where the JSON came from.

Tier 3 — Dynamic. User-supplied renderers handle routes that require custom logic — form submissions, APIs, CMSes, anything with mutable state. These are independent HTTP servers wired in as backends. m6 provides routing, caching, auth enforcement, and error handling around them.

The cache

This is the source of m6's performance. Every cacheable response is stored in RAM as a complete, ready-to-send unit:

  • The rendered HTML (or file bytes), already compressed to brotli or gzip
  • All HTTP response headers, pre-formed
  • The status code

On a cache hit, m6-http writes this blob directly to the network socket. No rendering, no compression, no template lookup, no file read, no allocation. The backend processes aren't contacted at all. For a typical static page or blog post, the effective server latency is measured in microseconds.

Cache hit path:
  request → cache lookup → write bytes to socket

Cache miss path:
  request → route match → backend → render → compress → cache → write to socket

Cache key: (path, query, content-encoding). Each encoding variant — brotli, gzip, identity — is cached independently. If a brotli-capable client is first, the brotli variant is cached. The next gzip-only client gets a fresh render, which is then cached as a separate entry.

What gets cached: Responses with Cache-Control: public. no-store and private are not cached. A 5xx and most 4xx responses are never cached, whatever their headers say.

Invalidation is one number. A cached entry leaves the cache in one of four ways: a successful state-changing request evicts the entry for its own path, its freshness lifetime ends (a page with no explicit max-age lives at most 24 hours), the site's generation changes and empties the whole cache, or the process restarts. A change to a file behind a page therefore does not reach readers until the generation changes.

The generation is a counter the source node owns. A publish is one POST /genid to m6-http: it reloads every backend on a Unix socket, flushes the cache and advances the counter, then answers with the new value. Tools that change content (a CMS renderer, a deploy script) send that request when they finish. There is no per-path map and nothing to keep in step with the files.

Backend pools and socket discovery

The socket glob in site.toml is the only configuration m6-http needs for a backend:

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-html"
sockets = "/run/m6/m6-html-*.sock"

m6-http expands the glob once, at start, so the backends start first (systemd After= on their units). Requests go to the pool's members in turn. A request whose connect fails tries the next member, and a backend that restarts on the same socket path serves again on its next turn. Scaling up means starting another instance on a new socket and restarting m6-http, with no change to the config.

Backends are only contacted on cache misses. A well-configured site with stable content will see backends contacted rarely — once per content version, per URL.

Auth

Routes declare require:

[[route]]
path    = "/admin"
backend = "m6-html"
require = "group:admins"

m6-http asks m6-auth's check socket about the caller's token before the request reaches any renderer, and only for routes that declare require. The check verifies the token's signature, kind, issuer, audience and expiry, and answers with the caller's current roles and groups. Renderers can read the caller's identity from the request dictionary (auth_username, auth_roles, auth_groups) for finer checks.

Reading files once

Every m6 process reads its configuration, site.toml, templates, params files and keys once, at start. A change to a configuration file takes a restart. A change to content does not: a publish is one POST /genid, which re-runs the start path in every backend and swaps the new site in only if it loads, so the old one keeps serving when it does not. A certificate renewal takes a restart of m6-http, which a certbot deploy hook does after each renewal.

Logging

Every process logs structured JSON to stdout. systemd captures it via journald. No log files in the site directory. No log rotation. No separate log daemon. journalctl -u m6-http -f is the interface.

Why one integrated system?

You could build something equivalent from separate tools — nginx as the proxy, Varnish as the cache, a template engine for rendering, a Markdown converter for content, a separate auth library. The parts exist and are individually excellent.

The cost is the integration surface. Each tool has its own config format, its own concept of a route, its own caching model, its own log format. Getting them to work together means writing glue, and debugging means knowing which layer handled (or dropped) each request.

m6 trades that flexibility for coherence. Because all the pieces share a common design — the same socket convention, the same config format, the same model of what a route is — the integration just works. A publish can be one request because every backend answers to the same site generation, and a cache that follows one number needs no glue. None of this requires configuration or glue.

Why Unix processes rather than a monolith?

The separate-process architecture isn't about flexibility for its own sake — it's about operational simplicity. Each process has one job, its own resource accounting, and its own restart boundary. A broken renderer doesn't take down the cache. Scaling a hot renderer means starting another instance on a new socket; m6-http finds it when it expands the pool's glob at its next start, with no config change.

The boundary between components is HTTP/1.1 over a Unix socket — utterly conventional. You can replace any component with anything that speaks that protocol. m6-core supplies the parts for writing a custom renderer in Rust, but any language works.

See the individual component posts for deeper dives: m6-http, m6-html and m6-core.

documents.body:
m6-http is the only process in an m6 deployment that listens on a public port. Its primary job is its in-memory response cache. Most requests in production never reach a backend. They're answered entirely from RAM.

Everything else — TLS termination, routing, auth enforcement, error page fetching — only runs when the cache can't answer the request.

The cache

flowchart TD
    Req["Request"] --> CacheHit{"Cache hit?"}
    CacheHit --"yes (common case)"--> ServeRAM["Write bytes to socket\n(no backend, no work)"]
    CacheHit --"no"--> AuthReq{"Auth required?"}
    AuthReq --"check refuses"--> Reject["401 / 403"]
    AuthReq --"check passes or no auth"--> RouteMatch{"Route match?"}
    RouteMatch --"no match"--> NotFound["404"]
    RouteMatch --"yes"--> Backend["Forward to backend"]
    Backend --> Cacheable{"Cacheable?"}
    Cacheable --"yes"--> CacheStore["Store in cache + return"]
    Cacheable --"no"--> Return["Return to client"]

A cache entry is a complete HTTP response, ready to write to the network:

  • Rendered HTML (or file bytes), already compressed to brotli or gzip
  • All response headers, pre-formed as a byte string
  • The status line

On a cache hit, m6-http does nothing except call write() on the socket. No template lookup, no file read, no compression, no backend contact, no allocation. For a typical page request, the server-side latency is a few microseconds.

Cache key: (path, query, content-encoding). Each encoding variant is cached independently — if a brotli client is first, the brotli variant is stored; the next gzip client triggers a fresh render which is cached as a separate entry.

What gets cached: Responses with Cache-Control: public. no-store and private are not cached. A 5xx and most 4xx responses are never cached, whatever their headers say.

The cache is stored behind an Arc, swapped for an empty one when the generation advances. The swap is non-blocking. In-flight requests that hold a reference to the old cache complete normally — they're reading from an immutable snapshot. The new snapshot is built and swapped in; the old one is freed when the last reader drops it.

Invalidation is one number

flowchart LR
    Publisher["publisher\n(CMS, deploy script)"] --"POST /genid"--> mhttp["m6-http\n(source node)"]
    mhttp --"POST /genid"--> Backends["every backend\non a Unix socket"]
    Backends --"204: reloaded"--> mhttp
    mhttp --> Swap["swap in an empty cache,\nadvance the generation ID"]

A cached entry leaves the cache in one of four ways: a successful state-changing request evicts the entry for its own path, its freshness lifetime ends, the site's generation changes and empties the cache, or the process restarts. A change to a file behind a page therefore does not reach the cache until one of those happens.

The generation is a counter the source node owns, written to $STATE_DIRECTORY/genid. A publish is one POST /genid, which needs a token with the claim [genid] write_require names, from a caller on loopback or an internal listener. m6-http runs four steps in its loop:

  1. Send POST /genid to every member of every socket pool. Each backend reads its config, templates and params again through its start path, keeps the old site if the new one does not load, and answers 204.
  2. Wait for every member, each under the backend timeout. A member that fails is logged at error with its socket path, and does not stop the sequence.
  3. In one step, rebuild the route table from the config loaded at start, swap the cache and the held error pages for empty ones, advance the ID and write it.
  4. Answer the POST with the new ID.

The ID changes only after every backend has the new content, so the cache cannot refill from a backend that still serves the old bytes under the new number. There is no per-path map and no sweep, and a request already holding an entry finishes on the content it took.

The event loop

m6-http runs a single-threaded event loop on one poll (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS). No Tokio. No async runtime. Just the poll, file descriptors, and explicit state machines.

The constraints are self-imposed and deliberate:

  • No heap allocation on the hot path
  • No unwrap() or expect() — every error is handled
  • No blocking calls in the event loop
  • The cache Arc is swapped atomically; never mutated in place

A single-threaded event loop is easier to reason about, easier to profile, and has predictable latency. There's no lock contention because there are no locks on the hot path.

HTTP/3 and QUIC

m6-http speaks HTTP/3 via quinn and HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 via rustls. QUIC connections share the same poll as TCP connections — the QUIC UDP socket is just another fd.

QUIC matters on real network paths with packet loss. On loopback, TCP wins the Happy Eyeballs race because the crypto handshake is slower. That's expected.

Routing (cache miss path only)

Route matching uses matchit, a radix tree router. Specificity rules: exact paths beat parameterised paths, longer paths beat shorter ones.

The routing decision runs only on cache misses:

  1. Auth required? Ask the auth check socket. 401 or 403 before any backend contact.
  2. Route match? Forward to backend pool.
  3. No match? 404 per configured error mode.
  4. Response cacheable? Store it. Next request is a cache hit.

Backend pools

Each [[backend]] is a pool of Unix sockets. m6-http expands the socket glob once, at start:

  • A glob that matches no socket at start stops m6-http with exit 2, so the backends start first (systemd After=)
  • A request whose connect fails tries the next member, and the client gets a 502 only when every member has failed
  • A backend that stops and restarts on the same socket path serves again on its next turn
  • Adding capacity means starting another instance on a new socket and restarting m6-http

Load balancing is plain round robin: each request takes the next member in turn, so every member takes the same share.

Auth enforcement

Routes with require are checked before forwarding:

[[route]]
path    = "/dashboard"
backend = "m6-html"
require = "group:staff"

The token is taken from Authorization: Bearer or the session cookie (header takes precedence) and sent to the check backend named by [auth] backend in the system config, which is m6-auth's check socket. m6-auth verifies the signature, kind, issuer, audience and expiry and answers with the caller's current roles and groups, and m6-http checks them against the require declaration. A role change therefore takes effect without a new token. The refusal is {"error":"unauthorised"} (401) or {"error":"forbidden"} (403) for an API client.

For browser clients with an expired token but a valid refresh cookie, m6-http transparently redirects through POST /auth/refresh and back to the original path. API clients always receive 401 directly.

Error handling

Three modes:

Mode Response
"status" Status code, empty body
"internal" Status code, m6-http-generated minimal HTML
"custom" Status code, error page fetched from [errors] path

In custom mode, m6-http makes a GET <errors-path>?status=N&from=<original-path> request to the error backend (typically m6-html), gets back a rendered HTML page, and returns it to the client with the original status code. If that fetch also fails, it falls back to internal mode. No recursion.

Reading files once

m6-http reads its configuration, site.toml, keys and certificates once, at start. A change to any of them takes a restart, and a certificate renewal takes a restart too, which the certbot deploy hook does. Content is different: a POST /genid rebuilds the route table from the config loaded at start (so a publish that adds a file a [[route_group]] glob matches gains its route), empties the cache and reloads every backend, with no restart. In-flight requests finish on the generation they started on.

Observability

Structured JSON to stdout. Every request logs: path, status, backend, latency in microseconds, cache hit/miss. Auth failures log at warn.

Periodic stats every 10 seconds: rps_avg, rps_peak, latency_p50_us, latency_p99_us, cache_hit_rate, backend_errors, pool_members.

journald captures everything. journalctl -u m6-http -f is all you need.

Running it

m6-http <site-dir> <system-config>

The system config holds the state of one node: its identity ([node]), its bind addresses and TLS paths ([server]), its check backend ([auth]) and the claims that gate /genid ([genid]). site.toml holds the settings every node shares, such as routes, backends, site identity and log level, and it lives alongside the content. m6-http logs a warning at start for each node key it finds in site.toml, naming the key and the file it belongs in.

# Development
m6-http . configs/system-dev.toml

# Production
m6-http /srv/my-blog /etc/m6/my-blog.toml

Exit codes: 0 clean shutdown, 1 runtime error, 2 config or usage error (before binding).

documents.body:
m6-html's application logic is one call and a loop:

let mut site = Site::load("m6-html", &[], &[], &TeraFactory);
// ... bind the socket, then the event loop: read a request,
// site.handle(&head), write the answer

It passes no code routes and no handler names, so every route it serves is a template from its config. Everything else — route matching, params loading, key merging, template rendering, compression, error handling, logging — comes from m6-core, the one crate every m6 service links. Understanding m6-core tells you everything about how m6-html works, and also how to write your own custom renderer for anything m6-html can't do on its own.

How m6-html renders a request

flowchart LR
    Req["Request"] --> PathMatch["Path\nmatching"]
    PathMatch --> ParamsLoad["Load params\nfiles"]
    ParamsLoad --> Merge["Merge global\nparams"]
    Merge --> Render["Render Tera\ntemplate"]
    Render --> Compress["Compress\n(br/gzip)"]
    Compress --> Resp["Response"]

  1. Path matching — the incoming path is matched against the routes declared in m6-html.conf. The first match wins. Parameterised paths extract named values (e.g. {stem} from /blog/hello-world).

  2. Params loading — each matched route lists params files. Path param values substitute into file paths: /blog/{stem} with stem=hello-world loads content/posts/hello-world.json. All params files are loaded and merged into a single JSON object.

  3. Global params merge — the global_params list at the top of the config (typically data/site.json) is merged in first. Route params overlay global params. Path params (from the URL) are added as top-level keys.

  4. Template render — the merged JSON object is passed to Tera as the context. The template specified in the route config is rendered.

  5. Compression — the rendered response is compressed per Accept-Encoding and per-MIME compression config. Brotli and gzip are supported.

  6. Response — status, headers, body sent back over the Unix socket.

Config

# configs/m6-html.conf

global_params = ["data/site.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/"
template = "templates/home.html"
params   = ["data/home.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/blog/{stem}"
template = "templates/post.html"
params   = ["data/posts.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/_errors"
template = "templates/error.html"
params   = []
cache    = "no-store"

The cache key on a route sets the Cache-Control header on responses. Default is public for rendered routes. Use no-store for the error route — you don't want a cached 404 page to be served for a valid path.

Tera templates

m6-html uses Tera, a template engine inspired by Jinja2. Template inheritance via {% extends %} and {% block %} works exactly as you'd expect.

One Tera behaviour worth knowing: {% set %} in a child template is silently discarded unless it's inside a {% block %}. If you need a derived variable in multiple blocks, set it independently in each block. This differs from Jinja2.

{% block title %}
  {%- set post = documents | filter(attribute="stem", value=stem) | first -%}
  {{ post.title }} · {{ site_name }}
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  {% set post = documents | filter(attribute="stem", value=stem) | first %}
  <h1>{{ post.title }}</h1>
  {{ post.body | safe }}
{% endblock %}

The safe filter marks the value as trusted HTML — necessary for rendered Markdown bodies.

Custom renderers with m6-core

Any route that requires logic beyond "render this template with this data" needs a custom renderer. m6-core supplies the parts of a service: routing, the request dictionary, templates, and the pieces of an event loop. The service writes its handlers and its own loop, so nothing is hidden in a framework.

A custom renderer declares its code routes as a constant and loads the site at start:

use m6_core::prelude::*;

const ROUTES: &[CodeRoute] = &[CodeRoute {
    pattern: "/hello/{name}",
    method: RouteMethod::Get,
}];

fn handle(req: &Request) -> Result<Response> {
    let name = req["name"].as_str().unwrap_or("world");
    Ok(Response::html(format!("<h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>")))
}

// In main: let mut site = Site::load("my-renderer", ROUTES, &[], &TeraFactory);
// then the loop, which answers each request with
//     Handled::Code(0, req) => site.finish(&req, handle(&req)?),

Site::load reads the config, site.toml and the templates once. site.handle matches a request and hands a code route back as Handled::Code(index, req), and site.finish adds the site-wide parts to the answer: a rendered template, Cache-Control, compression. docs/m6-app-anatomy.md in the m6 repository gives the whole loop for a one-route service, and every example's main.rs is that loop with its own handlers.

The Request type gives you the path params (req["name"]), the query, the form fields, the headers, the body and the caller's identity. The Response type covers the common cases: HTML, JSON, redirect, a rendered template. State, such as a mail relay or a database, is a plain value in main, owned by the one thread that runs the loop.

The socket naming convention is the same as m6-html: the config filename determines the socket path. configs/my-renderer.conf → /run/m6/my-renderer.sock. Declare it as a backend in site.toml:

[[backend]]
name    = "my-renderer"
sockets = "/run/m6/my-renderer*.sock"

And route to it:

[[route]]
path    = "/api/greet/{name}"
backend = "my-renderer"

m6-file

m6-file serves files from the filesystem. It shares the socket naming convention and CLI interface with m6-html, but has no templates and no params. Its one handler is registered in code under the name files, and configuration binds it to a path:

[[route]]
path    = "/assets/{*relpath}"
handler = "files"
root    = "assets/"

GET /assets/css/main.css → resolves to assets/css/main.css relative to the site directory. {*relpath} captures the rest of the path, slashes included. Path traversal is blocked: resolved paths must stay within root, .. sequences return 404, and symlinks outside root are not followed.

Compression

Both m6-html and m6-file compress responses per Accept-Encoding and per-MIME config. The defaults are sensible — text, HTML, CSS, JS compressed; images and fonts not. Override per MIME type:

[compression]
"text/html"  = { brotli = 6, gzip = 6 }
"image/jpeg" = { brotli = 0, gzip = 0 }

Compression level 0 means disabled for that MIME type. The compression decision is made once; subsequent requests for the same path and encoding are served from the m6-http cache.

documents.body:
This is the start of a seven-part guide that walks through every m6 example, from a bare static site to a full CMS running under systemd.

m6 is an integrated system for building and serving websites. It covers the whole journey — from writing content in Markdown, through template rendering, to an in-memory cache that serves pre-compressed responses directly from RAM. Each part is designed to work with the others: the renderer produces output the cache can serve directly, and one request to m6-http, POST /genid, reloads every backend and empties the cache when content changes. You could assemble something similar from nginx, Varnish, a template engine, and a Markdown converter, but you'd be managing four mental models and four integration surfaces. m6 is one system with one config format and one set of concepts across the whole stack.

In this guide:

  1. Prerequisites (this post)
  2. Example 01 — Static Site
  3. Example 02 — Blog with m6-md
  4. Example 03 — Contact Form
  5. Example 04 — Login and Protected Pages
  6. Example 05 — CMS Blog
  7. Example 06 — Production with systemd
  8. Example 07 — Dev to Production

Install the binaries

cargo install m6-http m6-html m6-file m6-auth-server m6-auth-cli

This installs five binaries to ~/.cargo/bin/:

  • m6-http — in-memory response cache, router, and reverse proxy. The only public-facing process. Most requests in production are answered entirely from its RAM cache — backends are only contacted on cache misses.
  • m6-html — renders HTML from Tera templates and JSON data files.
  • m6-file — serves files from the filesystem.
  • m6-auth-server — issues and verifies JWTs, answers m6-http's token checks, manages credentials.
  • m6-auth-cli — creates users, groups and API tokens in the auth database.

For the blog examples you'll also want m6-md, which converts Markdown files to the JSON format m6-html expects:

cargo install m6-md

Set up local TLS

m6-http always requires TLS. For local development, mkcert creates certificates trusted by your local browser — no cert warnings, no --insecure flags.

# Install the local CA (run once per machine)
mkcert -install

# Create a certificate for localhost
mkcert localhost 127.0.0.1

You do not need to run mkcert localhost yourself. Each example's dev.sh runs examples/dev-keys.sh, which writes the development certificate and auth keys to dev/ in ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-${TMPDIR:-$HOME/.cache}}/m6, a directory only you can use (mode 700; M6_DEV_HOME overrides the location) on first run. The example's configs/system-dev.toml names that directory as @M6_DEV_HOME@, because m6 reads absolute paths and expands no variables, and dev.sh writes a copy with the real path for m6-http to read. The mkcert -install step above is the only one you do by hand. If mkcert is missing, dev-keys.sh falls back to a self-signed certificate from openssl and your browser will warn about it.

Clone the examples

git clone https://github.com/m6/m6-examples
cd m6-examples

Now you have all five examples ready to run. Each is self-contained: its own site.toml, its own configs, its own templates and data. Each reads its TLS certificate from dev/ in that same private directory, written by examples/dev-keys.sh.

How the examples are structured

flowchart LR
    Browser --"HTTPS"--> mhttp["m6-http"]
    subgraph "Backends (Unix sockets)"
        mhtml["m6-html"]
        mfile["m6-file"]
        mauth["m6-auth"]
        custom["Custom Renderer"]
    end
    mhttp --"Unix socket"--> mhtml
    mhttp --"Unix socket"--> mfile
    mhttp --"Unix socket"--> mauth
    mhttp --"Unix socket"--> custom

Each example builds on the previous one. The directory names reflect the progression:

examples/
├── 01-static/
├── 02-blog/
├── 03-contact/
├── 04-auth/
├── 05-cms/
├── 06-systemd/
└── 07-dev-to-production/

Every example has a dev.sh that starts all the required processes and waits. Ctrl-C kills everything cleanly.

← m6-html and m6-core | Example 01 — Static Site →

documents.body:
Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 — Static Site → Example 02 → Example 03 → Example 04 → Example 05 → Example 06 → Example 07

examples/01-static/ is the base case. Templates, assets, and hand-authored JSON. No build step, no custom renderers. Three processes, one config each.

cd examples/01-static
./dev.sh
# open https://localhost:8443

Site directory

01-static/
├── site.toml
├── configs/
│   ├── m6-html.conf
│   └── m6-file.conf
├── templates/
│   ├── base.html
│   ├── home.html
│   ├── page.html
│   └── error.html
├── assets/
│   └── style.css
└── data/
    └── site.json

No binaries. No generated files. Everything you see is what you deploy.

site.toml

flowchart LR
    Browser --"HTTPS :8443"--> mhttp["m6-http"]
    mhttp --"/assets/*"--> mfile["m6-file\n(m6-file.conf)"]
    mhttp --"/, /about"--> mhtml["m6-html\n(m6-html.conf)"]

[site]
name   = "My Site"
domain = "localhost"

[errors]
mode             = "internal"
verbose_fallback = true

[log]
level  = "info"

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-html"
sockets = "/tmp/m6/m6-html*.sock"

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-file"
sockets = "/tmp/m6/m6-file*.sock"

[[route]]
path    = "/"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route]]
path    = "/about"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route]]
path    = "/_errors"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route_group]]
glob    = "assets/**/*"
path    = "/assets/{relpath}"
backend = "m6-file"

site.toml declares backends and routes. m6-http reads it. It holds nothing that differs between machines, so it has no [server] block. m6-html and m6-file have their own configs (below) that further describe how to handle each route on their side.

The [[route_group]] glob expands at startup: every file under assets/ becomes a routable URL. assets/style.css → /assets/style.css. No individual route declarations needed.

configs/system-dev.toml

[server]
bind     = "127.0.0.1:8443"
tls_cert = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev.pem"
tls_key  = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev-key.pem"

[node]
name = "dev"

The system config holds the state of the machine that runs m6-http: the node name, the address to listen on and the TLS certificate. It is the second argument to m6-http (see dev.sh below). The paths are absolute, and dev.sh runs examples/dev-keys.sh, which writes them to dev/ in a private per-user directory on first run. The config spells that directory @M6_DEV_HOME@, and dev.sh writes a copy with the real path and gives m6-http the copy. A production machine has its own system config with its own node name, bind address and certificate paths, and site.toml stays the same.

configs/m6-html.conf

global_params = ["data/site.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/"
template = "templates/home.html"
params   = []

[[route]]
path     = "/about"
template = "templates/page.html"
params   = ["data/about.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/_errors"
template = "templates/error.html"
params   = []
cache    = "no-store"

global_params are loaded for every request and merged into the template context first. Route params are loaded next and overlay globals. The template sees the merged result.

cache = "no-store" on the error route ensures m6-http never caches a 404 page and then serves it for a valid path.

configs/m6-file.conf

[[route]]
path = "/assets/{relpath}"
root = "assets/"

GET /assets/css/main.css → root = "assets/", relpath = "css/main.css" → resolves to assets/css/main.css relative to the site directory. Path traversal is blocked: .. sequences return 404, symlinks outside root are not followed.

All file responses are Cache-Control: public — m6-http caches them as pre-compressed byte blobs. After the first request, CSS and JS are served directly from RAM at the cost of a socket write. m6-file is not contacted again until the file changes on disk.

data/site.json

{
  "nav": [
    { "label": "Home",  "path": "/" },
    { "label": "About", "path": "/about" }
  ]
}

This file is the global_params source — merged into every template's context. Add any site-wide variables here: site_name, analytics IDs, feature flags, whatever every page needs.

templates/base.html

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>{% block title %}{{ site_name }}{% endblock %}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <nav>
    {% for item in nav %}
      <a href="{{ item.path }}">{{ item.label }}</a>
    {% endfor %}
  </nav>
  <main>{% block content %}{% endblock %}</main>
</body>
</html>

Tera template inheritance: {% extends "templates/base.html" %} in child templates, {% block content %} to fill the slot. Works like Jinja2 with one important difference: {% set %} at the top level of a child template is silently discarded — you must set variables inside the block where they're used.

templates/error.html

{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}{{ query.status }} · {{ site_name }}{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ query.status }} — {{ query.reason }}</h1>
  <p>The page <code>{{ query.path }}</code> could not be found.</p>
  <a href="/">Return home</a>
{% endblock %}

query is a built-in key that m6-html populates with the parsed query string from the URL. For error pages, m6-http calls /_errors?status=404&from=/missing-path — so query.status and query.from are available in the template.

dev.sh

#!/bin/bash
# dev.sh — start the 01-static stack for local development.
set -e

SITE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
M6="${M6:-$(cd "$SITE/../../.." && pwd)/m6}"
export PATH="$M6/target/release:$PATH"

# Development keys and state: a private per-user directory, see dev-home.sh.
. "$SITE/../dev-home.sh"
"$SITE/../dev-keys.sh"

# ── Clean up stale state ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mkdir -p /tmp/m6
lsof -ti :8443 2>/dev/null | xargs kill -9 2>/dev/null || true
sleep 0.3
rm -f /tmp/m6/m6-html.sock /tmp/m6/m6-file.sock

# ── Start services ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
M6_SOCKET_OVERRIDE=/tmp/m6/m6-html.sock \
    m6-html "$SITE" "$SITE/configs/m6-html.conf" &
HTML_PID=$!

M6_SOCKET_OVERRIDE=/tmp/m6/m6-file.sock \
    m6-file "$SITE" "$SITE/configs/m6-file.conf" &
FILE_PID=$!

trap 'kill $HTML_PID $FILE_PID $HTTP_PID 2>/dev/null; wait 2>/dev/null' EXIT

# Wait for backend sockets
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
    [ -S /tmp/m6/m6-html.sock ] && [ -S /tmp/m6/m6-file.sock ] && break
    sleep 0.2
done

m6-http "$SITE" "$(m6_conf "$SITE/configs/system-dev.toml")" &
HTTP_PID=$!

echo "Running at https://localhost:8443"
wait

The first lines load examples/dev-home.sh, which creates the private per-user directory (m6_conf writes a config copy with the real path into it), and run examples/dev-keys.sh, which writes the certificate named in configs/system-dev.toml into that directory if it does not exist yet. It uses mkcert when installed and falls back to a self-signed openssl certificate. The script then starts three background processes. trap kills them all on Ctrl-C. set -e aborts if any step fails.

Seeing a change

m6 reads its configuration, site.toml, templates and params files once, at start. After you change data/site.json or a template, stop the stack with Ctrl-C and run ./dev.sh again. m6-http keeps its cache in memory, so a restart also empties it.

A site that must show a change without a restart gives m6-http a [genid] table, and whatever changes the content sends POST /genid when it finishes: m6-http reloads every backend, empties its cache and answers with the new generation. Example 05 does this when an editor publishes.

Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 — Blog → Example 03 → Example 04 → Example 05 → Example 06 → Example 07

examples/02-blog/ adds a blog. Markdown source files in content/posts/ are processed by m6-md into a single JSON file at data/posts.json. m6-html serves the blog from that file. No per-post JSON files, no [[route_group]].

cd examples/02-blog
cargo install m6-md   # separate project, one-time install

# Generate posts.json from Markdown source, then start the site
m6-md content/posts/ --output data/posts.json
./dev.sh

To update content, re-run m6-md content/posts/ --output data/posts.json. m6-html reads data/posts.json once, at start, so restart the stack to see the change, or send POST /genid where the site has a generation (Example 05 does).

What's new

flowchart LR
    MDFiles["content/posts/\n*.md"] --> m6md["m6-md"]
    m6md --> JSON["data/posts.json"]
    JSON --> m6html["m6-html\n(Tera templates)"]
    m6html --> Browser

content/posts/ contains Markdown source files with TOML frontmatter. m6-md produces data/posts.json — a single JSON object with a documents array containing every post's metadata and rendered HTML body. m6 itself has no knowledge of Markdown.

Source file format

+++
title   = "Hello World"
date    = "2024-01-15"
summary = "A brief introduction to the blog."
tags    = ["rust", "web"]
+++

Post body in **Markdown**. GFM extensions supported: tables, strikethrough, footnotes, task lists, autolinks.

Any frontmatter key beyond title and date passes through to the JSON as-is. The body, stem, and path keys are reserved — m6-md sets them and will warn if you try to use them in frontmatter.

Files beginning with _ are skipped — use this for drafts and partials.

data/posts.json (produced by m6-md)

{
  "documents": [
    {
      "stem":    "hello-world",
      "path":    "/hello-world",
      "title":   "Hello World",
      "date":    "2024-01-15",
      "body":    "<p>Post body in <strong>Markdown</strong>...</p>",
      "summary": "A brief introduction to the blog.",
      "tags":    ["rust", "web"]
    }
  ]
}

Sorted by date descending. body is fully rendered HTML — m6-html just inserts it with the safe filter, no further processing. The write is atomic: m6-md writes to a .tmp file then renames, so m6-html never sees a partial file.

New routes in site.toml

[[route]]
path    = "/blog"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route]]
path    = "/blog/{stem}"
backend = "m6-html"

No [[route_group]]. The routes are fixed patterns — m6-html handles any /blog/{stem} and looks up the matching post in the params at request time.

New routes in configs/m6-html.conf

[[route]]
path     = "/blog"
template = "templates/post-index.html"
params   = ["data/posts.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/blog/{stem}"
template = "templates/post.html"
params   = ["data/posts.json"]

Both routes load the same file. The index template iterates documents. The post template filters by stem.

templates/post-index.html

{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Blog · {{ site_name }}{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>Blog</h1>
  {% for doc in documents %}
    <article>
      <h2><a href="/blog/{{ doc.stem }}">{{ doc.title }}</a></h2>
      <time>{{ doc.date }}</time>
      {% if doc.summary %}<p>{{ doc.summary }}</p>{% endif %}
    </article>
  {% endfor %}
{% endblock %}

Note: links use /blog/{{ doc.stem }} — not {{ doc.path }}. The path field from m6-md is /{stem} (without the /blog/ prefix). Use doc.stem to construct URLs in a blog context.

templates/post.html

{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}
  {%- set post = documents | filter(attribute="stem", value=stem) | first -%}
  {{ post.title }} · {{ site_name }}
{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  {% set post = documents | filter(attribute="stem", value=stem) | first %}
  <article>
    <h1>{{ post.title }}</h1>
    <time>{{ post.date }}</time>
    {{ post.body | safe }}
  </article>
{% endblock %}

stem is a built-in key provided by m6-html — the {stem} capture from the matched URL. The filter built-in finds the matching post from the documents array.

Important Tera behaviour: {% set %} at the top level of a child template is silently discarded. Set post independently inside each {% block %} where you need it. This differs from Jinja2.

Running m6-md

# One-shot generation
m6-md content/posts/ --output data/posts.json

# Re-run it whenever a post changes (with entr or similar)
find content/posts/ -name '*.md' | entr m6-md content/posts/ --output data/posts.json

m6-md has no watch mode of its own and does not signal the server. After it writes data/posts.json, the running m6-html still serves the file it read at start: restart it, or send POST /genid to m6-http where the site is a generation source.

Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 → Example 03 — Contact Form → Example 04 → Example 05 → Example 06 → Example 07

examples/03-contact/ introduces custom renderers. render-contact handles GET (renders the form) and POST (sends email via SMTP). Everything else — routing, caching, TLS — stays in the m6 layer.

cd examples/03-contact
cargo build --release -p render-contact
./dev.sh

What's a custom renderer?

flowchart LR
    Browser --"HTTPS"--> mhttp["m6-http"]
    mhttp --"/contact GET"--> mhtml["m6-html\n(template render)"]
    mhttp --"/contact POST"--> rc["render-contact\n(SMTP send)"]
    rc --"email"--> SMTP[("SMTP server")]

Any HTTP/1.1 server that listens on a Unix socket. m6-http finds it when it expands the pool's socket glob at start, and routes requests to it. A Rust renderer links m6-core, which supplies the parts of a service. The service writes its own event loop and its handlers.

render-contact/Cargo.toml

[package]
name    = "render-contact"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
m6-core    = { path = "../../../../m6/m6-core", features = ["email"] }
anyhow     = "1"
serde_json = "1"

The email feature compiles m6_core::email: an SMTP client the service's own loop drives without blocking.

render-contact/src/main.rs

State is a plain value built once at start. Here it is the mail relay, resolved and checked, and the two addresses:

use m6_core::email::{lettre, Relay, RelayConfig, Smtp};
use m6_core::prelude::*;

struct Global {
    relay: Relay,
    from:  String,
    to:    String,
}

fn load_state(site: &Site) -> Result<Global> {
    let config = site.user_config();
    let host = config["smtp"]["host"].as_str()
        .ok_or_else(|| Error::Other(anyhow::anyhow!("smtp.host missing")))?;
    // ... port, username, password, from and to are read the same way
    let relay = Relay::new(&RelayConfig {
        host: host.to_string(),
        port,
        starttls: tls,          // None only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1
        credentials,
        timeout: Duration::from_secs(20),
    }).map_err(|e| Error::Other(anyhow::anyhow!("{e}")))?;
    Ok(Global { relay, from, to })
}

The POST handler builds the message and starts the send on its connection slot's Smtp. It returns the page to show once the relay has accepted the message:

fn handle_post(req: &Request, global: &Global, smtp: &mut Smtp) -> Result<Response> {
    let name    = req.field("name")?;
    let email   = req.field("email")?;
    let text    = req.field("message")?;

    let msg = message(global, &name, &email, &text)?;
    smtp.start(&global.relay, &msg).map_err(|e| Error::Other(e.into()))?;

    Response::render_with("templates/contact.html", req, json!({"sent": true, "name": name}))
}

The routes are a constant, and main is the service's own loop:

const ROUTES: &[CodeRoute] = &[CodeRoute {
    pattern: "/contact",
    method: RouteMethod::Post,
}];

GET /contact is a template route in the configuration, so only the POST is code.

configs/render-contact.conf

global_params = ["data/site.json"]
secrets_file  = "/etc/m6/render-contact.toml"

[[route]]
path     = "/contact"
methods  = ["GET"]
template = "templates/contact.html"
params   = []
cache    = "no-store"

# Development defaults. In production these move to secrets_file and are
# deleted from here: a key set in both files is refused at start.
[smtp]
host     = "localhost"
port     = 1025
# The development relay speaks plain SMTP, which m6-core allows only to
# localhost. Production relays take STARTTLS: delete this line.
starttls = false
username = ""
password = ""
from     = "noreply@example.com"
to       = "owner@example.com"

secrets_file is merged in if the file exists. If absent (on dev machines), it's silently ignored and the [smtp] block above provides defaults. The path is absolute and safe to commit — it contains no secrets itself. methods = ["GET"] limits the template route to GET, because the POST is the code route in main.rs.

Production secrets file (on the server, not in version control):

# /etc/m6/render-contact.toml
[smtp]
host     = "smtp.example.com"
port     = 587
username = "user@example.com"
password = "live-smtp-password"

templates/contact.html

{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Contact · {{ site_name }}{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>Contact</h1>
  {% if sent %}
    <p>Message sent. Thanks, {{ name }}!</p>
  {% else %}
    <form method="post" action="/contact">
      <label>Name    <input type="text"  name="name"    required></label>
      <label>Email   <input type="email" name="email"   required></label>
      <label>Message <textarea           name="message" required></textarea></label>
      <button type="submit">Send</button>
    </form>
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}

Same template handles both states — sent is absent on GET, true after a successful POST.

New entries in site.toml

[[backend]]
name    = "render-contact"
sockets = "/run/m6/render-contact*.sock"

[[route]]
path    = "/contact"
backend = "render-contact"

The socket name is derived from the config filename: configs/render-contact.conf → /run/m6/render-contact.sock.

Updated dev.sh

./target/release/render-contact "$SITE" "$SITE/configs/render-contact.conf" &

Added alongside the existing m6-html, m6-file, and m6-http lines. The renderer starts and creates its socket, and m6-http finds it when it expands the pool's glob at its own start, so the backends start before m6-http.

How the loop sends mail

main loads the site, builds its state with load_state and runs the loop with one Smtp slot per connection slot:

  1. Site::load reads the config (the renderer conf and the secrets overlay), site.toml and the templates, once. A start that cannot build its state prints why and exits 2.
  2. The loop waits on one poll for the listener, the signals, every client and every mail connection.
  3. A POST /contact arrives as Handled::Code(0, req). The handler starts the send, and the loop holds the "sent" page and registers the mail socket under the slot's odd token.
  4. Each time the mail socket fires, smtp.drive() advances the exchange without blocking: Ok(None) means keep waiting, Ok(Some(())) means the relay accepted the message and the loop sends the held page, and Err answers 500 with the cause.
  5. A relay that takes longer than its deadline answers 504, and a client that leaves while its message is in flight drops the exchange.

State is a plain value in main, owned by the one thread that runs the loop, so it needs no lock. A slow relay holds one client's answer and never the loop.

Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 → Example 03 → Example 04 — Auth → Example 05 → Example 06 → Example 07

examples/04-auth/ adds m6-auth. Members-only pages are protected behind a login form. The JWT is stored in an HttpOnly cookie — the browser sends it automatically on every request, JavaScript cannot read it.

cd examples/04-auth
./setup.sh   # generates keys, creates first admin user
./dev.sh
# login at https://localhost:8443/login

Key generation and bootstrap (setup.sh)

#!/bin/bash
set -e
SITE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"

# Development keys and state: a private per-user directory, see dev-home.sh.
. "$SITE/../dev-home.sh"
"$SITE/../dev-keys.sh"

# Create first admin user — database created automatically if absent
m6-auth-cli "$(m6_conf "$SITE/configs/m6-auth.conf")" user add admin --role admin

echo "Setup complete. Start the server with ./dev.sh"

Run setup.sh once per environment. The private key stays on the server and signs the tokens. m6-auth-server verifies them when m6-http asks.

configs/m6-auth.conf

[storage]
path = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/04-auth/auth.db"

[tokens]
access_ttl  = 900       # 15 minutes
refresh_ttl = 2592000   # 30 days
issuer      = "localhost"

[keys]
private_key = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/auth.pem"
public_key  = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/auth.pub"

m6-auth manages its own SQLite database at storage.path. The access token is short-lived (15 min); the refresh token is long-lived (30 days).

New entries in the system config

[auth] names the backend m6-http asks who a caller is, and it belongs in the system config (configs/system-dev.toml) and not in site.toml, because it describes this node. The backend is the check socket of m6-auth-server, declared in site.toml below.

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

New entries in site.toml

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-auth"
sockets = "/run/m6/m6-auth*.sock"

# The check socket carries POST /check. Its name is the login socket's with a
# `check-` prefix, which keeps it out of the login glob above.
[[backend]]
name    = "m6-auth-check"
sockets = "/run/m6/check-m6-auth*.sock"

[[route]]
path    = "/login"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route]]
path    = "/auth/login"
backend = "m6-auth"

[[route]]
path    = "/auth/logout"
backend = "m6-auth"

[[route]]
path    = "/auth/refresh"
backend = "m6-auth"

[[route]]
path    = "/members"
backend = "m6-html"
require = "group:members"

[[route]]
path    = "/members/{page}"
backend = "m6-html"
require = "group:members"

The [auth] block tells m6-http which backend to ask who a caller is: the check socket of m6-auth-server. Routes with require are enforced before m6-html is ever contacted.

The cookie scheme

sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant mhttp as m6-http
    participant mauth as m6-auth
    participant mhtml as m6-html

    Browser->>mhttp: GET /members (no cookie)
    mhttp->>Browser: 302 /login?next=/members
    Browser->>mhttp: POST /auth/login (credentials)
    mhttp->>mauth: forward
    mauth->>Browser: 302 /members + Set-Cookie: session, refresh
    Browser->>mhttp: GET /members (session cookie)
    mhttp->>mhttp: verify JWT locally (no network)
    mhttp->>mhtml: forward
    mhtml->>Browser: members page

On successful login, m6-auth sets two HttpOnly cookies:

Set-Cookie: session=<access_token>;  HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/;             Max-Age=900
Set-Cookie: refresh=<refresh_token>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/auth/refresh; Max-Age=2592000

The session cookie is sent on every request — m6-http sends it to the check socket, which verifies it and answers with the caller's current roles and groups. The refresh cookie is sent only to POST /auth/refresh due to its restricted Path. JavaScript can read neither cookie. No XSS exposure of tokens.

Session expiry and transparent refresh

When the session cookie expires:

  1. Next request to a protected route → m6-http finds no valid access token
  2. Browser request (Accept: text/html)? Check for refresh cookie
  3. Refresh cookie present and valid? → redirect to POST /auth/refresh
  4. m6-auth issues new cookies → redirect back to original path
  5. User never sees a login page

If the refresh token is also expired, or absent: redirect to /login?next=<original-path>. API clients (non-text/html Accept) receive 401 directly throughout.

templates/login.html

{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Login · {{ site_name }}{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>Login</h1>
  {% if query.error %}
    <p class="error">Invalid username or password.</p>
  {% endif %}
  <form method="post" action="/auth/login">
    <input type="hidden" name="next" value="{{ query.next }}">
    <label>Username <input type="text"     name="username" required autofocus></label>
    <label>Password <input type="password" name="password" required></label>
    <button type="submit">Login</button>
  </form>
{% endblock %}

The hidden next field carries the original destination through the form POST. m6-auth validates that next is a relative path before using it — no open redirect.

m6-auth handles POST /auth/login (form-encoded) and either:

  • Success → sets cookies, 302 to next
  • Failure → 302 to /login?error=invalid&next=<next>

templates/members.html

{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Members · {{ site_name }}{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>Members Area</h1>
  <p>Welcome. This page is only visible after login.</p>
  <form method="post" action="/auth/logout">
    <button type="submit">Logout</button>
  </form>
{% endblock %}

Logout is a plain form POST — no JavaScript. m6-auth clears both cookies and redirects to /.

Managing users with m6-auth-cli

# Add a user
m6-auth-cli configs/m6-auth.conf user add alice --group members

# Set a password
m6-auth-cli configs/m6-auth.conf user passwd alice

# Add to a group
m6-auth-cli configs/m6-auth.conf group add-member members alice

# List users
m6-auth-cli configs/m6-auth.conf user ls

m6-auth-cli reads the same conf as m6-auth-server. It writes directly to the SQLite database, and a change takes effect on the next check, because POST /check reads the database's current roles and groups.

How m6-http enforces require

For each request to a route with require:

  1. Extract JWT from Authorization: Bearer header, or the session cookie (header wins)
  2. Send it to the check backend (POST /check on m6-auth-server's check socket), which verifies the signature, kind, issuer, audience and expiry
  3. Check the require declaration, group:<name> or role:<name>, against the roles and groups the check answered with
  4. Reject with 401 (no or invalid token) or 403 (insufficient claims): JSON for an API client, a redirect to /login for a browser
  5. Valid? Forward request with token intact

Renderers receive the verified identity as keys in the request context (auth_username, auth_roles, auth_groups) and can perform additional fine-grained checks.

Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 → Example 03 → Example 04 → Example 05 — CMS Blog → Example 06 → Example 07

examples/05-cms/ is the full system. A public blog served at maximum speed from the m6-http RAM cache. An auth-protected CMS renderer for creating, editing, and publishing posts. No database — posts are JSON files on disk.

cd examples/05-cms
./setup.sh           # keys, first admin user
cargo build --release -p render-cms
./dev.sh
# CMS at https://localhost:8443/cms (login required)
# Blog at https://localhost:8443/blog (public, cached)

Site directory

05-cms/
├── site.toml
├── configs/
│   ├── system-dev.toml
│   ├── m6-html.conf
│   ├── m6-file.conf
│   ├── m6-auth.conf
│   └── render-cms.conf
├── templates/
│   ├── base.html
│   ├── home.html
│   ├── post-index.html
│   ├── post.html
│   ├── login.html
│   ├── error.html
│   └── cms/
│       ├── dashboard.html
│       └── editor.html
├── assets/
├── content/
│   ├── posts/     ← published JSON (one file per post)
│   └── drafts/    ← draft JSON (never publicly routable)
├── keys/
└── render-cms/
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/main.rs

site.toml

[site]
name   = "My Blog"
domain = "localhost"

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-html"
sockets = "/run/m6/m6-html-*.sock"

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-file"
sockets = "/run/m6/m6-file-*.sock"

[[backend]]
name    = "m6-auth"
sockets = "/run/m6/m6-auth-*.sock"

[[backend]]
name    = "render-cms"
sockets = "/run/m6/render-cms-*.sock"

# ── Public routes — no auth, fully cached ────────────────────────

[[route]]
path    = "/"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route]]
path    = "/blog"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route_group]]
glob    = "content/posts/*.json"
path    = "/blog/{stem}"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route_group]]
glob    = "assets/**/*"
path    = "/assets/{relpath}"
backend = "m6-file"

[[route]]
path    = "/_errors"
backend = "m6-html"

# ── Auth endpoints — public ──────────────────────────────────────

[[route]]
path    = "/login"
backend = "m6-html"

[[route]]
path    = "/auth/login"
backend = "m6-auth"

[[route]]
path    = "/auth/logout"
backend = "m6-auth"

[[route]]
path    = "/auth/refresh"
backend = "m6-auth"

# ── CMS — all protected, never cached ───────────────────────────

[[route]]
path    = "/cms"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/cms/edit/{stem}"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/cms/new"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/api/drafts"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/api/drafts/{stem}"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/api/publish/{stem}"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/api/unpublish/{stem}"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route]]
path    = "/api/posts/{stem}"
backend = "render-cms"
require = "group:editors"

[[route_group]] with content/posts/*.json handles routing for individual posts. m6-http expands the glob when it builds its route table at start. A post file a publish adds is routed because the publish ends with POST /genid, and site.toml itself is read once, at start: an edit to it takes a restart.

site.toml has no [auth] because the backend it names belongs to one node. It goes in the system config.

configs/system-dev.toml

[server]
bind     = "127.0.0.1:8443"
tls_cert = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev.pem"
tls_key  = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev-key.pem"

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

[genid]
read_require  = "role:genid-read"
write_require = "role:genid-write"

[node]
name = "dev"

[auth] names the backend m6-http asks who a caller is: the check socket of m6-auth, declared as the m6-auth-check backend in site.toml (sockets = "/tmp/m6/check-m6-auth*.sock"). [genid] makes this node the source of the site's generation ID and names the claims that gate /genid: a token with the genid-write role may publish. Declare each table in one file only. A key in the file that does not own it stops m6-http at start with exit 2.

render-cms/Cargo.toml

[package]
name    = "render-cms"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
m6-core        = { path = "../../../../m6/m6-core" }
serde_json     = "1"
comrak         = { version = "0.21", default-features = false }
base64         = "0.22"
rustls-pemfile = "2"

m6-core is the one m6 crate a service links. It supplies routing, the request dictionary, templates and the pieces of an event loop. The service writes its own main, which is the loop, and its handlers.

render-cms/src/main.rs

The routes are a constant, in the order the match below reads them. Site::load compiles them at start, and each request that one of them answers comes back as Handled::Code(index, req):

const ROUTES: &[CodeRoute] = &[
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/contact",              method: RouteMethod::Get },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/contact",              method: RouteMethod::Post },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/cms",                  method: RouteMethod::Get },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/cms/new",              method: RouteMethod::Get },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/cms/edit/{stem}",      method: RouteMethod::Get },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/api/drafts",           method: RouteMethod::Post },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/api/drafts/{stem}",    method: RouteMethod::Patch },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/api/publish/{stem}",   method: RouteMethod::Post },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/api/unpublish/{stem}", method: RouteMethod::Post },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/api/drafts/{stem}",    method: RouteMethod::Delete },
    CodeRoute { pattern: "/api/posts/{stem}",     method: RouteMethod::Delete },
];

main is the service's own event loop: start, run, stop. It loads the site, binds the socket, opens the signal descriptor, and then waits on one poll for the listener, the signals and every connection. Nothing in the run phase blocks. docs/m6-app-anatomy.md in the m6 repository walks through the loop line by line, and main.rs in this example is that loop with one addition: a publish waits on a POST /genid, which the same loop drives.

A handler answers Answer::Now(response), or Answer::AfterPublish(response) when it changed the site's files. The loop holds an AfterPublish answer, sends POST /genid to m6-http on the connection slot's own client, and writes the answer when m6-http has replied:

fn handle_publish(req: &Request) -> Result<Answer> {
    let stem         = req["stem"].as_str().ok_or(Error::NotFound)?;
    let draft_path   = format!("content/drafts/{}.json", stem);
    let publish_path = format!("content/posts/{}.json", stem);

    let mut post = req.read_json(&draft_path)?;
    post["stem"]         = json!(stem);
    post["path"]         = json!(format!("/blog/{}", stem));
    post["published_at"] = json!(now_iso8601());

    req.write_json_atomic(&publish_path, &post)?;
    update_index(req)?;
    let _ = fs::remove_file(req.site_path(&draft_path));

    Ok(Answer::AfterPublish(Response::json(json!({"published": true, "path": post["path"]}))))
}

fn handle_unpublish(req: &Request) -> Result<Answer> {
    let stem         = req["stem"].as_str().ok_or(Error::NotFound)?;
    let publish_path = format!("content/posts/{}.json", stem);
    let draft_path   = format!("content/drafts/{}.json", stem);

    let mut post = req.read_json(&publish_path)?;
    post["draft"] = json!(true);
    req.write_json(&draft_path, &post)?;
    let _ = fs::remove_file(req.site_path(&publish_path));
    update_index(req)?;

    Ok(Answer::AfterPublish(Response::json(json!({"unpublished": true}))))
}

The handlers do not touch site.toml: m6 services read their files once, at start, and a touch reloads nothing. The POST /genid is what makes every backend read the new content.

configs/render-cms.conf

global_params = ["data/site.json"]

[[route]]
path  = "/cms"
cache = "no-store"
# ... one entry per route above

[genid]
url        = "https://localhost:8443/genid"
connect    = "127.0.0.1:8443"
token_file = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/05-cms/genid-write.token"
ca_file    = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/ca.pem"
timeout_ms = 10000

[genid] names the publish URL, the address to connect to, the file holding a token with the genid-write role (dev.sh mints it with m6-auth-cli ... token create), the certificate to trust (a development node signs its own; in production leave ca_file out and the system's certificate store is used) and how long a publish may take. A missing or empty token file stops the renderer at start.

CMS API

Method Path Action
POST /api/drafts Create draft → returns {"stem":"..."}
PATCH /api/drafts/{stem} Update draft fields
DELETE /api/drafts/{stem} Delete draft permanently
POST /api/publish/{stem} Publish draft → moves to posts, then POST /genid
POST /api/unpublish/{stem} Move published post back to drafts
DELETE /api/posts/{stem} Delete published post permanently

The dashboard shows Edit / Delete for drafts and View / Edit / Unpublish / Delete for published posts. The editor defaults the date field to today for new posts.

The publish flow

  1. Editor saves draft → POST /api/drafts or PATCH /api/drafts/{stem} writes content/drafts/{stem}.json
  2. Editor clicks Publish → POST /api/publish/{stem}:
    • render-cms renders markdown → HTML, writes content/posts/{stem}.json
    • render-cms rebuilds data/posts.json index
    • render-cms sends POST /genid to m6-http, which reloads every backend, flushes its cache and advances the generation — /blog/{stem} becomes live
    • the answer to the editor waits for that request, so a post reported as published is live
    • render-cms deletes content/drafts/{stem}.json
  3. Browser goes to /blog/{stem}
  4. m6-http: cache empty after the flush, cache miss → m6-html renders → m6-http caches
  5. Every subsequent request to /blog/{stem}: cache hit — RAM only
sequenceDiagram
    participant Editor
    participant rcms as render-cms
    participant Disk
    participant mhttp as m6-http
    participant mhtml as m6-html
    participant Browser

    Editor->>rcms: PATCH /api/drafts/my-post (save draft)
    Editor->>rcms: POST /api/publish/my-post
    rcms->>Disk: write content/posts/my-post.json
    rcms->>mhttp: POST /genid (write token)
    mhttp->>mhtml: reload
    mhttp-->>rcms: 200, new generation (cache flushed)
    rcms->>Editor: {"published": true}
    Editor->>Browser: open /blog/my-post
    Browser->>mhttp: GET /blog/my-post
    mhttp->>mhtml: cache miss, render
    mhtml->>mhttp: response
    mhttp->>Browser: page (now cached)

Performance profile

Request type Latency
Public post (cached) < 1 ms — RAM only
Public post (cache miss) ~5 ms — m6-html reads JSON, renders, caches
CMS dashboard one check of the token by m6-auth, then render-cms reads the posts and drafts directories
Publish one atomic file write, then one POST /genid whose answer the editor waits for

The public blog path never touches disk after the first request.

dev.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -e
SITE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
trap 'kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null' EXIT

# keys, auth database and the publisher token (examples/dev-token.sh)
m6-html        "$SITE" "$SITE/configs/m6-html.conf" &
m6-file        "$SITE" "$SITE/configs/m6-file.conf" &
m6-auth-server "$SITE" "$(m6_conf "$SITE/configs/m6-auth.conf")" &   # login and check sockets
"$EXAMPLES/target/release/render-cms" "$SITE" "$(m6_conf "$SITE/configs/render-cms.conf")" &
# the source node writes its generation ID under STATE_DIRECTORY
STATE_DIRECTORY="$M6_DEV_HOME/05-cms/state" m6-http "$SITE" "$(m6_conf "$SITE/configs/system-dev.toml")" &

echo "Running at https://localhost:8443"
echo "CMS at    https://localhost:8443/cms"
wait

← Example 04 — Login and Protected Pages | Example 06 — Production with systemd →
