documents.body:
Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 → Example 03 → Example 04 → Example 05 → Example 06 — systemd → Example 07

examples/06-systemd/ takes the CMS blog from example 05 and runs it properly under systemd. Every process is a unit. Ordering, restart policy, log capture, socket directory permissions, deploy workflow, and horizontal scaling are all covered.

Server preparation

# Dedicated user — no login shell, no home directory
useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin m6

# Site directory — owned by m6 user
mkdir -p /var/www/my-blog
chown m6:m6 /var/www/my-blog

# Auth keys, kept root-owned because systemd reads them as a credential
mkdir -p /etc/m6
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -pkeyopt ec_param_enc:named_curve -out /etc/m6/auth.pem
openssl pkey -in /etc/m6/auth.pem -pubout -out /etc/m6/auth.pub
chmod 600 /etc/m6/auth.pem
chmod 600 /etc/m6/auth.pub

# TLS certificate via Let's Encrypt
certbot certonly --standalone -d example.com
# Outputs /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem
#         /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem
# The m6-http unit delivers both through LoadCredential

# System config — this node's own state, passed to m6-http as its second argument
cat > /etc/m6/my-blog.toml << 'TOML'
[server]
bind     = "0.0.0.0:443"
tls_cert = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-cert.pem"
tls_key  = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-key.pem"

[node]
name = "origin"

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

[genid]
read_require  = "role:genid-read"
write_require = "role:genid-write"
TOML
chown root:m6 /etc/m6/my-blog.toml
chmod 640 /etc/m6/my-blog.toml

systemd copies the certificate and key into m6-http's credential directory when the unit starts, so the hook restarts m6-http after each renewal:

# /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/m6-http-restart.sh, mode 0755
#!/bin/sh
systemctl restart m6-http

Until it runs, m6-http keeps serving the previous certificate.

Deploy the site directory

# From your development machine
rsync -av --delete \
  --exclude 'content/drafts/' \
  --exclude 'keys/' \
  examples/05-cms/ \
  user@example.com:/var/www/my-blog/

# On the server, fix ownership after rsync
chown -R m6:m6 /var/www/my-blog

content/posts/ (published posts) and keys/ are excluded — these live exclusively on the server.

Unit files

flowchart TD
    net["network.target"]
    net --> mhtml["m6-html.service"]
    net --> mfile["m6-file.service"]
    net --> mauth["m6-auth.service"]
    net --> rcms["render-cms.service"]
    mhtml --> mhttp["m6-http.service"]
    mfile --> mhttp
    mauth --> mhttp
    rcms --> mhttp

One unit per process. Renderers follow the same pattern; only ExecStart and Description differ.

/etc/systemd/system/m6-html.service

[Unit]
Description=m6-html renderer
Documentation=https://github.com/mgrosvenor/m6
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=m6
Group=m6

RuntimeDirectory=m6
RuntimeDirectoryMode=0750
RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes

ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-html \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    /var/www/my-blog/configs/m6-html.conf

Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2

StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=m6-html

NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/run/m6
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/my-blog /etc/m6

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

/etc/systemd/system/m6-file.service

[Unit]
Description=m6-file renderer
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=m6
Group=m6
RuntimeDirectory=m6
RuntimeDirectoryMode=0750
RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes

ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-file \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    /var/www/my-blog/configs/m6-file.conf

Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=m6-file
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/run/m6
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/my-blog

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

/etc/systemd/system/m6-auth.service

[Unit]
Description=m6-auth service
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=m6
Group=m6
RuntimeDirectory=m6
RuntimeDirectoryMode=0750
RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes

ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-auth-server \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    /etc/m6/m6-auth.conf

LoadCredential=auth.pem:/etc/m6/auth.pem
LoadCredential=auth.pub:/etc/m6/auth.pub
StateDirectory=m6-auth
StateDirectoryMode=0700

Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=m6-auth
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/run/m6
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/my-blog /etc/m6

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

m6-auth's keys come from the two LoadCredential lines, and its database lives in /var/lib/m6-auth, which StateDirectory=m6-auth creates.

/etc/systemd/system/render-cms.service

[Unit]
Description=render-cms custom renderer
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=m6
Group=m6
RuntimeDirectory=m6
RuntimeDirectoryMode=0750
RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes

ExecStart=/var/www/my-blog/bin/render-cms \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    /etc/m6/render-cms.conf

# The token that lets render-cms publish with POST /genid. It arrives as
# /run/credentials/render-cms.service/genid-write.token
LoadCredential=genid-write.token:/etc/m6/genid-write.token

Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=render-cms
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/run/m6 /var/www/my-blog/content
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/my-blog /etc/m6

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

The render-cms binary lives in /var/www/my-blog/bin/ — deployed alongside the site, not installed system-wide.

/etc/systemd/system/m6-http.service

[Unit]
Description=m6-http reverse proxy and cache
Documentation=https://github.com/mgrosvenor/m6
After=network.target m6-html.service m6-file.service m6-auth.service render-cms.service

[Service]
Type=simple
User=m6
Group=m6
RuntimeDirectory=m6
RuntimeDirectoryMode=0750
RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes

WorkingDirectory=/var/www/my-blog

ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-http /var/www/my-blog /etc/m6/my-blog.toml

LoadCredential=tls-cert.pem:/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem
LoadCredential=tls-key.pem:/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem

# The source node writes the site's generation ID here
StateDirectory=m6-http
StateDirectoryMode=0700

Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=m6-http

AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/run/m6 /var/www/my-blog/logs
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/my-blog /etc/m6

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

After= orders the start: m6-http expands each pool's socket glob once, at start, and a glob that matches no socket stops it with exit 2, so the backends must have bound their sockets first. m6-auth-server binds two sockets, m6-auth.sock for login and check-m6-auth.sock for the token check m6-http asks on every protected route and on /genid.

StateDirectory=m6-http gives m6-http /var/lib/m6-http, where the source node writes the site's generation ID, because ProtectSystem=strict makes the rest of the disk read-only.

The render-cms unit delivers the publisher token with LoadCredential, as /run/credentials/render-cms.service/genid-write.token, and starts from /etc/m6/render-cms.conf. The site's configs/render-cms.conf is the development config: its [genid] table names the development token and CA. Build the production copy from it, keeping the routes and replacing only that table, which is the last one in the file:

sed '/^\[genid\]/,$d' /var/www/my-blog/configs/render-cms.conf > /etc/m6/render-cms.conf
cat >> /etc/m6/render-cms.conf << 'CONF'
[genid]
url        = "https://example.com/genid"
connect    = "127.0.0.1:443"
token_file = "/run/credentials/render-cms.service/genid-write.token"
timeout_ms = 10000
CONF
chown root:m6 /etc/m6/render-cms.conf
chmod 640 /etc/m6/render-cms.conf

Production leaves ca_file out, so the system's certificate store is trusted.

Mint the publisher token once the auth database exists, after the first start of m6-auth:

m6-auth-cli /etc/m6/m6-auth.conf user add publisher --role genid-write --password "$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
m6-auth-cli /etc/m6/m6-auth.conf token create publisher --name publish --ttl-days 90 > /etc/m6/genid-write.token
chmod 600 /etc/m6/genid-write.token

Without --ttl-days a token lasts 365 days. This one expires 90 days after it is minted. From then on /genid answers 401 to it, and the CMS can no longer publish. To rotate it before that, mint a new token the same way into a new file, move it over /etc/m6/genid-write.token, run systemctl restart render-cms (systemd copies the credential in when the unit starts), then revoke the old one: m6-auth-cli /etc/m6/m6-auth.conf token ls publisher lists the tokens with their ids, and token revoke <id> ends one. A cache node follows the site with a reader token of its own, one user per node (reader-edge-a, and so on, with the genid-read role), minted the same way and rotated the same way with systemctl restart m6-http-cache. See example 09's setup-origin.sh.

Install and start

cp examples/06-systemd/systemd/*.service /etc/systemd/system/

systemctl daemon-reload

systemctl enable m6-html m6-file m6-auth render-cms m6-http
systemctl start  m6-html m6-file m6-auth render-cms m6-http

systemctl status m6-html m6-file m6-auth render-cms m6-http

Verify

# Check m6-http is listening
ss -tlnp | grep :443

# Check all sockets appeared
ls -la /run/m6/
# Expected:
# /run/m6/m6-html.sock
# /run/m6/m6-file.sock
# /run/m6/m6-auth.sock
# /run/m6/render-cms.sock

# Smoke test
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://example.com/
# 200
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://example.com/cms
# 302 (redirect to /login)

Logs

# Follow all m6 processes together
journalctl -f -u m6-http -u m6-html -u m6-file -u m6-auth -u render-cms

# Structured log processing
journalctl -u m6-http -o cat | jq .

# Errors only
journalctl -u m6-http -p err

# Between timestamps
journalctl -u m6-http --since "2024-01-15 09:00" --until "2024-01-15 10:00"

Deploy updates

# Template, data or content changes — rsync, then publish
# m6 reads its files at start, so the site is told to read them again with one
# POST /genid (loopback, with the publisher token); a site.toml edit needs a restart
rsync -av --delete \
  --exclude 'content/drafts/' \
  --exclude 'keys/' \
  examples/05-cms/ user@example.com:/var/www/my-blog/

# Binary changed — deploy and restart just that unit
cargo build --release -p render-cms
rsync target/release/render-cms user@example.com:/var/www/my-blog/bin/
ssh user@example.com systemctl restart render-cms
# m6-http connects to the socket again on its next turn — other units unaffected

# TLS cert renewal — certbot's deploy hook restarts m6-http
certbot renew

Horizontal scaling

Add a second m6-html instance with no change to the site config:

# Create a second config (content identical to m6-html.conf)
cp /var/www/my-blog/configs/m6-html.conf \
   /var/www/my-blog/configs/m6-html-2.conf

# Copy and edit the unit
cp /etc/systemd/system/m6-html.service \
   /etc/systemd/system/m6-html-2.service
# Edit ExecStart to reference m6-html-2.conf, update Description and SyslogIdentifier

systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable m6-html-2
systemctl start  m6-html-2

# /run/m6/m6-html-2.sock appears
# m6-http expands the pool's glob at start, so restart it to add the member
systemctl restart m6-http
# Traffic now goes to both instances in turn (round robin)

Scale back down:

systemctl stop m6-html-2
# A request that finds the socket gone tries the next member, so one refused
# connect is the whole cost until the next m6-http restart drops it

Crash recovery

Restart=on-failure with RestartSec=2 handles crashes automatically. During the 2-second restart window a request to that pool tries the next member, and the client gets a 502 only when every member has failed. A backend that restarts on the same socket path serves again on its next turn.

# Simulate a crash
systemctl kill -s KILL m6-html

# Watch systemd restart it
journalctl -u m6-html -f

← Example 05 — CMS Blog | Example 07 — Dev to Production →

documents.body:
Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 → Example 03 → Example 04 → Example 05 → Example 06 → Example 07 — Dev to Production → Example 08

examples/07-dev-to-production/ is the complete workflow for taking a site from local development to a production server. The same site directory runs in both environments — the system config holds the node state that differs.

The split

site.toml — version controlled, deployed with the site, no secrets:

[site]
name   = "My Blog"
domain = "example.com"

[log]
level  = "info"

[errors]
mode = "internal"

# All backends and routes — identical in dev and production
[[backend]]
name    = "m6-html"
sockets = "/run/m6/m6-html-*.sock"
# ... full backend and route table as in example 05

site.toml has no bind address, no certificate paths and no [auth]. Those describe one node, so they live in the system config. m6-http logs a warning at start for each node key it finds in site.toml.

configs/system-dev.toml — development system config, version controlled:

# The node state in development.
# Committed to the repo — contains no secrets. @M6_DEV_HOME@ stands for the
# per-user directory the dev scripts create (dev-home.sh); dev.sh copies this
# file with the real path filled in.
[server]
bind     = "127.0.0.1:8443"
tls_cert = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev.pem"
tls_key  = "@M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev-key.pem"

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

[genid]
read_require  = "role:genid-read"
write_require = "role:genid-write"

[node]
name = "dev"

/etc/m6/my-blog.toml — production system config, on the server only:

[node]
name = "web-1"

[server]
bind     = "0.0.0.0:443"
tls_cert = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-cert.pem"
tls_key  = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-key.pem"

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

[genid]
read_require  = "role:genid-read"
write_require = "role:genid-write"

The system config holds the state of one node: its identity ([node]), its binds and TLS paths ([server]), its check backend ([auth]) and the claims that gate /genid ([genid]). Each table goes in one file only, and a key in the file that does not own it stops m6-http at start with exit 2. Everything else comes from site.toml unchanged.

configs/render-contact.conf — version controlled, uses local mock values:

secrets_file = "/etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml"
# On dev machines /etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml doesn't exist
# — silently ignored, [smtp] values below are used.

global_params = ["data/site.json"]

[[route]]
path     = "/contact"
template = "templates/contact.html"
params   = []
cache    = "no-store"

[smtp]
host     = "localhost"
port     = 1025
username = ""
password = ""
from     = "dev@localhost"
to       = "dev@localhost"

/etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml — on the server only:

[smtp]
host     = "smtp.postmarkapp.com"
port     = 587
username = "live-api-token"
password = "live-api-token"
from     = "noreply@example.com"
to       = "owner@example.com"

When secrets_file points to a file that exists, it's merged in and wins on conflict. When absent (on dev machines), silently ignored. The secrets_file path itself is safe to commit.

First-time server setup

# Create system user
useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin m6

# Create site directory
mkdir -p /var/www/my-blog
chown m6:m6 /var/www/my-blog

# Generate production auth keys
mkdir -p /etc/m6
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -pkeyopt ec_param_enc:named_curve -out /etc/m6/auth.pem
openssl pkey -in /etc/m6/auth.pem -pubout -out /etc/m6/auth.pub
chown m6:m6 /etc/m6/auth.pem /etc/m6/auth.pub
chmod 600 /etc/m6/auth.pem

# Create production system config
cat > /etc/m6/my-blog.toml << 'TOML'
[node]
name = "web-1"

[server]
bind     = "0.0.0.0:443"
tls_cert = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-cert.pem"
tls_key  = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-key.pem"

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

[genid]
read_require  = "role:genid-read"
write_require = "role:genid-write"
TOML
chown root:m6 /etc/m6/my-blog.toml
chmod 640 /etc/m6/my-blog.toml

# Create SMTP secrets
cat > /etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml << 'TOML'
[smtp]
host     = "smtp.postmarkapp.com"
port     = 587
username = "live-api-token"
password = "live-api-token"
from     = "noreply@example.com"
to       = "owner@example.com"
TOML
chown root:m6 /etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml
chmod 640 /etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml

# Obtain TLS certificate
certbot certonly --standalone -d example.com

# Install systemd units
cp examples/07-dev-to-production/systemd/*.service /etc/systemd/system/
systemctl daemon-reload

# Deploy site (see deploy.sh below), then:
systemctl enable m6-html m6-file m6-auth render-cms m6-http
systemctl start  m6-html m6-file m6-auth render-cms m6-http

The m6-http unit for this example

The only difference from example 06 is ExecStart passes the production system config path explicitly:

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-http \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    /etc/m6/my-blog.toml

Renderer units are identical to example 06 — they take only two positional args and use secrets_file for credentials.

deploy.sh

#!/bin/bash
# Run from your development machine
set -e

SERVER="user@example.com"
REMOTE_SITE="/var/www/my-blog"

rsync -av --delete \
  --exclude 'content/drafts/' \
  --exclude 'keys/' \
  --exclude '*.pem' \
  --exclude '*.pub' \
  --exclude 'target/' \
  ./ "$SERVER:$REMOTE_SITE/"

ssh "$SERVER" chown -R m6:m6 "$REMOTE_SITE"

if [[ "$1" == "--binary" ]]; then
  cargo build --release -p render-cms
  rsync target/release/render-cms "$SERVER:$REMOTE_SITE/bin/"
  ssh "$SERVER" systemctl restart render-cms
fi

echo "Deployed."
# new content is read when the site's generation advances (POST /genid)

For template, data and content changes: ./deploy.sh, then one POST /genid (the CMS sends it when an editor publishes), which reloads every backend and empties the cache. A site.toml or system config change takes a restart of m6-http. For renderer binary changes: ./deploy.sh --binary — only render-cms restarts; all other units and the m6-http cache are unaffected.

Dev vs production at a glance

Development Production
m6-http invocation m6-http $SITE "$(m6_conf $SITE/configs/system-dev.toml)" m6-http /var/www/my-blog /etc/m6/my-blog.toml
[server] bind 127.0.0.1:8443 0.0.0.0:443
TLS cert @M6_DEV_HOME@/dev/dev.pem /run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-cert.pem
SMTP localhost:1025 (mock) smtp.postmarkapp.com:587
SMTP credentials inline in renderer config /etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml via secrets_file
[auth] backend m6-auth-check m6-auth-check
publisher token ([genid] token_file in the renderer config) @M6_DEV_HOME@/07-dev-to-production/genid-write.token /run/credentials/render-cms.service/genid-write.token
System config configs/system-dev.toml (in repo) /etc/m6/my-blog.toml (on server)
Process manager dev.sh systemd
Logs terminal stdout journald

Routes, templates, backends and log settings are identical. The same site.toml runs in both environments.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Version Controlled"
        sitetoml["site.toml"]
        sysdev["system-dev.toml"]
        rcconf["render-contact.conf"]
    end
    subgraph "Server Only"
        prodsys["/etc/m6/my-blog.toml"]
        prodsec["/etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml"]
    end
    sitetoml --> HTTP["m6-http"]
    sysdev -. "dev" .-> HTTP
    prodsys -. "prod" .-> HTTP
    rcconf --> RC["render-contact"]
    prodsec -. "prod only" .-> RC

Checking what's in effect

# See the effective merged config — useful when debugging prod behaviour
m6-http /var/www/my-blog /etc/m6/my-blog.toml --dump-config

# Output shows [server] values from /etc/m6/my-blog.toml,
# everything else from site.toml:
#
# [server]
# bind     = "0.0.0.0:443"
# tls_cert = "/run/credentials/m6-http.service/tls-cert.pem"
# ...

Common mistakes

Forgetting the system config argument:

m6-http /var/www/my-blog
# Exit 2 — second argument required in production

Putting secrets in renderer config instead of secrets_file:

# Wrong — committed to repo
[smtp]
password = "live-api-token"   # in configs/render-contact.conf

# Right — in /etc/m6/contact-secrets.toml, referenced by secrets_file

Deploying over data/posts.json — wipes published posts:

# Wrong
rsync -av ./ user@server:/var/www/my-blog/

# Right — always exclude server-managed state
rsync -av \
  --exclude 'content/drafts/' \
  --exclude 'keys/' \
  ./ user@server:/var/www/my-blog/

Editing site.toml directly on the server:

# Wrong — next deploy overwrites it
ssh server vim /var/www/my-blog/site.toml

# Right — edit locally and deploy
# Server-specific overrides belong in /etc/m6/my-blog.toml

That completes the guide. For the architecture deep-dives, see the architecture overview, the m6-http internals post, and the m6-html and m6-core post.

← Example 06 — Production with systemd | Example 08 — Global Deployment →

Guide series: Prerequisites → Example 01 → Example 02 → Example 03 → Example 04 → Example 05 → Example 06 → Example 07 → Example 08: Global Deployment

examples/09-global-deployment/ shows how to spread a single m6 site across six nodes worldwide using WireGuard as an encrypted backbone and GeoDNS to route each user to their nearest edge.

Architecture

graph TD
    DNS["GeoDNS\n(ClouDNS)"] -->|Oceania| ORIGIN
    DNS -->|Americas West| EDGEA
    DNS -->|Americas East| EDGEB
    DNS -->|Americas Central| EDGEC
    DNS -->|Europe| EDGED
    DNS -->|Asia| EDGEE

    subgraph "Origin"
        ORIGIN["m6-http\nbind=0.0.0.0:443 TLS\nh2c_bind=10.0.0.1:80"]
        BACKENDS["m6-html · m6-file\nm6-auth · render-cms"]
        ORIGIN --> BACKENDS
    end

    subgraph "WireGuard 10.0.0.0/24"
        EDGEA["edge-a\n10.0.0.2"]
        EDGEB["edge-b\n10.0.0.3"]
        EDGEC["edge-c\n10.0.0.4"]
        EDGED["edge-d\n10.0.0.5"]
        EDGEE["edge-e\n10.0.0.6"]
    end

    EDGEA -->|H2C| ORIGIN
    EDGEB -->|H2C| ORIGIN
    EDGEC -->|H2C| ORIGIN
    EDGED -->|H2C| ORIGIN
    EDGEE -->|H2C| ORIGIN

One origin runs all backend services. Five cache nodes (edge-a, edge-b, edge-c, edge-d, edge-e) each run a single m6-http instance that proxies everything upstream.

The cache nodes are pure HTTP proxies. They hold no content, no auth database, no CMS. All writes go through the origin. Reads are served locally when cached.

Why H2C over WireGuard?

The cache nodes talk to the origin over H2C (HTTP/2 cleartext) on WireGuard. WireGuard already encrypts the tunnel end-to-end, so adding TLS on top would mean:

  • Double encryption, which wastes CPU on both ends
  • Certificate management for internal-only endpoints
  • No benefit, because WireGuard peers are authenticated by public key

H2C on WireGuard gives you HTTP/2 multiplexing (multiple in-flight requests per connection, header compression) with WireGuard's encryption and zero-round-trip reconnect. It is faster and simpler than an internal TLS setup.

Node roles

Origin

One m6-http instance handles both the public edge and the H2C backbone via two fields in the system config:

configs/origin.toml:

[server]
bind     = "0.0.0.0:443"
tls_cert = "/run/credentials/m6-http-origin.service/tls-cert.pem"
tls_key  = "/run/credentials/m6-http-origin.service/tls-key.pem"
h2c_bind = "10.0.0.1:80"
internal_binds = ["10.0.0.1:80"]
internal_peers = ["10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.3", "10.0.0.4", "10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.6"]

[auth]
backend = "m6-auth-check"

[genid]
read_require  = "role:genid-read"
write_require = "role:genid-write"

[node]
name = "origin"
  • bind: public HTTPS on all interfaces, served to end users and Oceania GeoDNS traffic
  • h2c_bind: cleartext HTTP/2 on the WireGuard interface, only reachable from cache nodes
  • internal_binds: declares the h2c listener internal, so m6-http trusts the client address a cache node forwards. m6-http refuses to start with h2c_bind set and no internal_binds.
  • internal_peers: the addresses the cache nodes connect from. m6-http closes a connection from any other address, so trust does not depend on the firewall alone.
  • [auth]: the check backend m6-http asks who a caller is belongs to this node, so it lives in its system config.
  • [genid]: the origin is the source of the site's generation ID. A publish is one POST /genid to it. It needs StateDirectory= in its unit, and a cache node follows the ID on its heartbeat.

Both listeners share the same site config and backend Unix sockets in /run/m6/*.sock.

Cache nodes

Each cache node runs one m6-http instance with:

configs/cache-<node>.toml for the TLS bind and the node-specific cert path:

# edge-d example
[server]
bind     = "0.0.0.0:443"
tls_cert = "/run/credentials/m6-http-cache.service/tls-cert.pem"
tls_key  = "/run/credentials/m6-http-cache.service/tls-key.pem"

[node]
name = "edge-d"

configs/cache-site.toml is identical on every cache node:

[[backend]]
name = "origin"
url  = "h2c://10.0.0.1:80"

[[route]]
path    = "/"
backend = "origin"

# ... full route table mirrors origin-site.toml ...

# CMS and auth routes always bypass cache
[[route]]
path      = "/cms"
backend   = "origin"
require   = "group:editors"
cache     = "no-store"

The cache = "no-store" on CMS and auth routes ensures writers always reach the origin. Every other route can be served from the cache node's in-memory HTTP cache.

WireGuard hub-and-spoke

The origin is the WireGuard hub. Each cache node is a spoke.

wireguard/origin-wg0.conf:

[Interface]
Address    = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820
PrivateKey = <origin-private-key>

[Peer]  # edge-a
PublicKey  = <edge-a-public-key>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32

[Peer]  # edge-b
PublicKey  = <edge-b-public-key>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.3/32

# ... edge-d (10.0.0.5), edge-e (10.0.0.6), edge-c (10.0.0.4)

wireguard/edge-a-wg0.conf (spoke):

[Interface]
Address    = 10.0.0.2/24
PrivateKey = <edge-a-private-key>

[Peer]  # origin
PublicKey           = <origin-public-key>
Endpoint            = example.com:51820
AllowedIPs          = 10.0.0.1/32
PersistentKeepalive = 25

PersistentKeepalive = 25 keeps the NAT mapping alive on VPS providers that drop idle UDP sessions.

systemd units

Two units on the origin, one on each cache node:

Origin (one unit for both listeners):

# m6-http-origin.service
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-http \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    /etc/m6/origin.toml

origin.toml has both bind (TLS) and h2c_bind (WireGuard backbone), one process with two listening sockets.

Cache nodes (one unit, parameterised via EnvironmentFile):

# m6-http-cache.service
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/m6/node-config
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/m6-http \
    /var/www/my-blog \
    ${NODE_CONFIG}

/etc/m6/node-config on each cache node contains just:

NODE_CONFIG=/etc/m6/cache.toml

The same .service file deploys identically to all five edges. Only the environment file differs per node.

TLS certificates

Cache nodes need per-node certificates for their own hostname (edge-a.example.com, edge-d.example.com, and so on). Certbot DNS challenge is the easiest path for wildcard certs:

# One wildcard covers all nodes
certbot certonly --dns-cloudflare \
    -d "*.example.com" \
    --dns-cloudflare-credentials /etc/m6/cloudflare.ini

Or use individual per-node certs with standalone certbot on each node.

The deploy hook restarts m6-http, and systemd copies the new certificate into the unit when it starts:

# /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/m6-http-restart.sh
systemctl restart m6-http-origin

On a cache node the hook restarts m6-http-cache.

GeoDNS with ClouDNS

ClouDNS GeoDNS routes each user to their nearest node by returning a different A record per geographic region:

Region Hostname resolves to
Oceania + default example.com
Americas West edge-a.example.com
Americas East edge-b.example.com
Americas Central edge-c.example.com
Europe edge-d.example.com
Asia edge-e.example.com

The actual A records point to each server's public IP. GeoDNS is purely a routing layer. It has no knowledge of m6 or your content.

All six names (example.com, edge-a.example.com, and so on) are A records that ClouDNS serves conditionally based on the resolver's location.

First-time setup

Origin:

./setup-origin.sh example.com admin@example.com

The script installs WireGuard, certbot, and ufw, generates auth keys in /etc/m6/, patches the domain into the system config, and installs systemd units.

Each cache node:

# On the cache node
./setup-cache-node.sh edge-a edge-a.example.com wireguard/edge-a-wg0.conf

Then sync the WireGuard keys (generate with wg genkey | tee privkey | wg pubkey > pubkey on each node, patch into the .conf files, then wg set wg0 peer <pubkey> ... or restart wg-quick).

Deploy

# From your dev machine, push content to the origin
./deploy.sh user@example.com

# From the origin, push static assets to cache nodes
# (cache nodes hold no server-side content, but having templates
#  locally avoids a round-trip for error pages)
rsync -av --delete \
  --exclude 'content/drafts/' --exclude 'keys/' \
  /var/www/my-blog/ root@edge-a.example.com:/var/www/my-blog/

Because cache nodes proxy everything to the origin, you only need to keep static assets in sync. Blog content is always fetched live from the origin.

Local demo

Run the entire 6-node topology on one machine using loopback addresses:

cd examples/09-global-deployment
./dev.sh

This starts:

Instance Address Role
Origin https://127.0.0.1:9001 Public TLS for direct access + CMS
Origin H2C backbone http://127.0.0.1:9000 Cache-node backbone (internal)
Cache edge-a https://127.0.0.1:9002 edge-a proxy
Cache edge-b https://127.0.0.1:9003 edge-b proxy
Cache edge-c https://127.0.0.1:9004 edge-c proxy
Cache edge-d https://127.0.0.1:9005 edge-d proxy
Cache edge-e https://127.0.0.1:9006 edge-e proxy

One m6-http process on the origin handles both listeners (bind for TLS, h2c_bind for H2C). All five cache instances proxy back to 127.0.0.1:9000 over plain H2C (mirroring production WireGuard). You can hit any of the five TLS ports and get the same blog served from the same origin.

TLS uses a mkcert self-signed cert generated on first run. The CMS is available at https://127.0.0.1:9001/cms (login: admin / admin).

Cost

Six entry-level VPS nodes (~$6/month each on most providers) gives you global reach for ~$36/month total. There is no CDN contract, no origin shield fee, no per-GB egress pricing beyond what the VPS provider charges (typically 1–2 TB/month included). The WireGuard backbone traffic between nodes is minimal. It is only cache misses and CMS writes.
